# The Public Rejects OMB's Federal Financial Assistance Rule

OMB Director Russell Vought is seen after testifying during the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing on oversight of the Office of Management and Budget, in Rayburn building on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images)

On May 29, the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) [proposed a comprehensive overhaul of 2 CFR Part 200](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/29/2026-10817/regulation-for-federal-financial-assistance), commonly known as the Uniform Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance. Since 2013, this framework has governed how federal agencies administer federal grants, cooperative agreements, and financial assistance across the United States. With over $1 trillion in such federal assistance subject to 2 CFR 200—much of that going towards programs that support state and local governments, tribes, universities, nonprofits, public authorities, school districts, healthcare organizations, small businesses, and research institutes—the outcome of the proposed rule affects a large sector of the US economy. About $150 billion of the assistance takes the form of research and development grants that support America’s investment in science and technology.

The proposed rule seeks to elevate the text from administrative guidance to a binding government-wide regulation, centralizing rulemaking authority within the OMB itself. Key provisions introduce mandatory pre-issuance reviews of all discretionary awards by political appointees to ensure alignment with administration policy priorities. Additionally, the proposal expands agency discretion to terminate existing awards and restricts funding for collaborations with specific foreign entities.

## The response of the science and technology community

In a June editorial titled "[Another red alert for American science](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aej3572)," *Science* Editor-in-Chief Holden Thorp argues that the proposed White House Office of Management and Budget rule change represents an effort to bypass congressional intent and starve federal research. Thorp states that by introducing political review into the funding pipeline, the rule effectively overrides the established scientific peer-review process. He emphasizes that allowing political appointees to select, cut, or terminate research awards threatens the structural foundations of American scientific discovery, turning independent research allocation into an instrument of executive policy.

The scientific and academic communities responded with widespread concern, organizing advocacy campaigns to highlight the risks these changes pose to research independence and administrative stability. Organizations such as the [American Physical Society](https://www.aps.org/initiatives/advocate-amplify/policy/federal-grants-rule-change) and the [American Geophysical Union](https://agu.quorum.us/campaign/163877/) mobilized their members to submit public feedback using custom platforms to assist the public with writing their responses.

So, how did the public respond, and how effective were these campaigns? To find out, we analyzed every comment on the docket with [an open-source pipeline we built for reading public comments at scale](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/). We downloaded all of the comments from regulations.gov, including the text of attached letters and PDFs, and used an LLM to process each one and record its position on the rule, the specific concerns it raised, and what kind of person or organization submitted it. A second pass double-checked those labels, while a separate step grouped near-identical submissions into form-letter campaigns, and another linked each comment to the sections of the rule it cites. The results feed the interactive dashboard we draw on below.

Between May 29 and July 9, roughly 51,000 comments were posted to [regulations.gov](https://www.regulations.gov/document/OMB-2026-0034-0001) (and over 200,000 more had been received but not yet published). The verdict on public sentiment is clear and lopsided: about 94 percent oppose the proposed rule and only 6 percent support it, with fewer than one percent marked as unclear. The opposition is overwhelmingly grassroots rather than orchestrated. Form letters make up only about 16 percent of all comments (roughly 8,400 comments across 210 distinct campaigns), and only about one in eight opposing comments came from a form-letter campaign. Support for the rule, by contrast, was almost entirely organized: nearly nine in ten supportive comments (about 2,500) came from a single form-letter campaign. Opponents mostly wrote their own comments; supporters mostly signed the same form-letter.

The commenters span many sectors, but individuals dominate: about 39,000 comments (77 percent) came from unaffiliated individuals, and another 7,900 from individual researchers and academics. Roughly 3,300 came from patients, families, and health advocates. Organized institutions were a small share by count but a notable one by voice, including scientific and professional societies (about 70), universities and research institutions (about 30), and advocacy nonprofits (nearly 280). The offices of at least 14 elected officials sent in letters of opposition, including one by [Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) with 125 co-signers](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-38282). The letter sent by Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) [directly to OMB Director Russell Vought](https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/news/majority/sen-collins-asks-omb-to-withdraw-parts-of-grant-rule-extend-comment-period) was not included in the collection.

#### Our content delivered to your inbox.

#### Thank you!

When we look at what commenters actually objected to, two themes dominate: the politicization of grant decisions, raised in roughly two-thirds of all comments, and the fear that the rule would sideline scientific peer review, raised in more than half. The counts alone understate the intensity of the objections by the community.

One federally funded scientist [wrote](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-0132) that: “scientists doing the vetting of projects is the core of a non partisan program, allowing partisan non-scientists oversight is a mistake our research communities will take generations to recover from.” The [American Society of Naturalists](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-0996) warned that the rule “would require that senior political appointees personally review and approve every discretionary research grant for consistency with presidential policy priorities.” Objections often named specific provisions: one physician-researcher [singled out §200.205](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-0502), “which would require a senior political appointee to personally review and approve discretionary grants, with authority to override the outcome of scientific peer review.”

Not every objection was about science. The [Southern Environmental Law Center](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-15961) focused on process, arguing that “only 45 days for public comment on a rule of this magnitude … is inadequate,” noting the proposal runs more than 400 pages and binds 41 other federal agencies. One concerned citizen, a food-bank volunteer, [highlighted the economic significance of the proposed rule:](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-42160) “The proposal affects well over $1 trillion in annual Federal grants and cooperative agreements, and affects every State, every Tribe, and most major nonprofits, universities, hospitals, and federally funded private industry. OMB has not even attempted to quantify the impacts on any of them. I fear that many of the small, local food banks that I work with would get lost in this new structure, and because of it, thousands of people in my city would go hungry.” We note that the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within OMB determined that the rule was [economically non-significant](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eoDetails?rrid=1292261) when it completed its review.

Supporters were not only fewer but narrower: almost all of the roughly 2,900 supportive comments cited preventing waste, fraud, and abuse (WFA) and little else—the [Immigration Accountability Project](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-12742), for instance, applauded the rule’s new requirement that federal grant recipients use the E-Verify program. The relatively few supporters that wrote their own comments offered nuanced perspective, with a mixture of support for reducing WFA and recommendations for revisions, such as those submitted by the [City of Lago Vista, Texas](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-36630): “The City supports efforts to improve oversight of federal expenditures. However, reimbursement procedures should be administered in a manner that does not unnecessarily delay payments...”

The comments cluster around a handful of provisions. Section [200.205](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.205), the pre-issuance review of discretionary awards by political appointees, drew the most attention, cited in about 6,900 comments. Section [200.340](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.340), which expands the authority to terminate active awards, was second with about 5,900. Other frequently cited provisions set new limits on allowable costs, including Sections [200.461](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.461) and [200.432](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.432) (each cited in more than 3,000 comments).

## The resounding public response is a categorical ‘no’, so what’s next?

Taken together, the record is striking. Tens of thousands of scientists, clinicians, and ordinary citizens wrote in their own words to warn OMB that putting political appointees in charge of which research gets funded would erode the quality and independence of federally funded science. The comments in support were far fewer and narrower. Under the notice-and-comment process, OMB is now required to review these comments and respond to every substantive argument they raise before it can issue a final rule. The timeline is aggressive for OMB to analyze and respond to comments with only a few weeks between the close of comments on July 13 and the proposed effective date of October. We encourage reviewers [to use our tool to simplify analysis.](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/)

Finally, there should be an opportunity for the public to request meetings with OMB under Executive Order 12866 to discuss the rule when the OIRA starts its final review. Interested parties should monitor [reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eoPackageMain) should that option become available to the public.

# 公眾反對 OMB 的聯邦財務援助規則

OMB 主任 Russell Vought 於 2026 年 6 月 30 日星期二，在雷本大樓出席眾議院撥款委員會金融服務暨一般政府小組委員會、就管理與預算局監督議題作證後現身。（Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images）

5 月 29 日，白宮管理與預算局（Office of Management and Budget, OMB）[提議全面修訂《聯邦法規彙編》第 2 篇第 200 部分](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/29/2026-10817/regulation-for-federal-financial-assistance)，這套規範通常稱為《聯邦財務援助統一指南》。自 2013 年以來，這套架構一直規範美國各聯邦機關如何在全國管理聯邦補助、合作協議與財務援助。受 2 CFR 200 規範的這類聯邦援助超過 1 兆美元，其中很大一部分流向支持州與地方政府、原住民族部落、大學、非營利組織、公共機構、學區、醫療組織、小型企業與研究機構的計畫，因此這項擬議規則的結果將影響美國經濟的一大部門。其中約 1,500 億美元援助是以研發補助形式提供，支撐美國對科學與科技的投資。

這項擬議規則試圖將原本屬於行政指引的文字，提升為具有拘束力、適用於整個政府的法規，並把規則制定權集中到 OMB 本身。關鍵條文包括：要求所有裁量性補助案在核發前，都必須由政治任命人員審查，以確保符合現任政府的政策優先事項。此外，這項提案也擴大各機關終止既有補助案的裁量權，並限制與特定外國實體合作時可取得的資金。

## 科學與科技界的回應

在六月一篇題為「[美國科學的又一次紅色警報](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aej3572)」的社論中，*Science* 總編輯 Holden Thorp 主張，白宮管理與預算局（Office of Management and Budget）提出的規則修訂，是試圖繞過國會意旨，並讓聯邦研究經費枯竭。Thorp 指出，這項規則把政治審查引入資金核撥流程，實質上推翻了既有的科學同儕審查制度。他強調，若允許政治任命官員選擇、刪減或終止研究補助，將威脅美國科學發現的結構性根基，把獨立的研究資源分配變成執行部門政策的工具。

科學與學術社群對此表達廣泛憂慮，並組織倡議行動，凸顯這些變更對研究獨立性與行政穩定性造成的風險。[美國物理學會](https://www.aps.org/initiatives/advocate-amplify/policy/federal-grants-rule-change)與[美國地球物理聯盟](https://agu.quorum.us/campaign/163877/)等組織動員會員提交公開意見，並透過客製化平台協助公眾撰寫回應。

那麼，公眾如何回應？這些倡議行動又有多有效？為了找出答案，我們用[自行建立、用來大規模閱讀公開意見的開源流程](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/)分析了該案卷中的每一則留言。我們從 regulations.gov 下載所有意見，包括附件信函與 PDF 的文字，並使用大型語言模型（LLM）處理每一則意見，記錄其對這項規則的立場、提出的具體憂慮，以及提交意見者屬於哪一類個人或組織。第二輪處理會再次檢查這些標籤；另一個獨立步驟則將近乎相同的提交內容歸類為制式信件倡議活動，並再由另一個步驟把每則意見連結到其引用的規則段落。這些結果匯入了下文所依據的互動式儀表板。

5 月 29 日至 7 月 9 日之間，約有 51,000 則意見被張貼到 [regulations.gov](https://www.regulations.gov/document/OMB-2026-0034-0001)（另有超過 200,000 則已收到、但尚未公開）。公眾情緒的結論很清楚，而且一面倒：約 94% 反對這項擬議規則，只有 6% 支持，標示為不明確的不到 1%。反對意見壓倒性地是草根自發，而不是組織動員。制式信只占所有意見約 16%（約 8,400 則意見，來自 210 個不同的行動），而反對意見中只有約八分之一來自制式信行動。相較之下，對這項規則的支持幾乎全是有組織的：近九成支持意見（約 2,500 則）來自單一制式信行動。反對者多半自己撰寫意見；支持者多半簽署同一份制式信。

留言者橫跨許多領域，但以個人為主：約 39,000 則意見（77%）來自無隸屬單位的個人，另有 7,900 則來自個別研究者與學者。約 3,300 則來自病患、家屬與健康倡議者。以數量來看，組織機構所占比例不高，但其聲量值得注意，包括科學與專業學會（約 70 個）、大學與研究機構（約 30 個），以及倡議型非營利組織（近 280 個）。至少 14 位民選官員的辦公室送出反對信，包括一封由 [Jamie Raskin 眾議員（民主黨，馬里蘭州）與 125 位共同連署人](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-38282)提出的信。Susan Collins 參議員（共和黨，緬因州）[直接寄給 OMB 主任 Russell Vought](https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/news/majority/sen-collins-asks-omb-to-withdraw-parts-of-grant-rule-extend-comment-period) 的信，並未納入這份彙整。

#### 我們的內容送到你的收件匣。

#### 謝謝！

當我們檢視留言者實際反對的內容時，有兩個主題最突出：一是補助決策政治化，約三分之二的意見提到這點；二是擔心這項規則會讓科學同儕審查被邊緣化，超過半數意見提到這點。單看數字，還低估了這個社群反對的強烈程度。

一位接受聯邦資助的科學家[寫道](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-0132)：「由科學家審核計畫，是非黨派計畫的核心；讓帶有黨派立場的非科學人士監督，是我們研究社群需要好幾個世代才能恢復的錯誤。」[美國自然學家學會（American Society of Naturalists）](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-0996)警告，這項規則「將要求高階政治任命官員親自審查並核准每一筆裁量性研究補助，以確認其是否符合總統的政策優先事項。」反對意見也常點名特定條文：一位醫師研究者[特別點名 §200.205](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-0502)，「該條將要求高階政治任命官員親自審查並核准裁量性補助，並有權推翻科學同儕審查的結果。」

並非所有反對意見都與科學有關。[南方環境法律中心（Southern Environmental Law Center）](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-15961)聚焦於程序，主張「這種規模的規則只給 45 天公眾意見徵詢期……並不充分」，並指出提案篇幅超過 400 頁，且約束另外 41 個聯邦機關。一位憂心的公民、同時也是食物銀行志工，[強調這項擬議規則的經濟重要性：](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-42160)「這項提案影響每年遠超過 1 兆美元的聯邦補助與合作協議，並影響每一州、每一個部落，以及大多數主要非營利組織、大學、醫院和接受聯邦資助的私營產業。OMB 甚至沒有嘗試量化對其中任何一方的影響。我擔心許多我合作的小型地方食物銀行會在這個新架構中被淹沒；也因此，我所在城市將有成千上萬的人挨餓。」我們注意到，OMB 內的資訊與法規事務辦公室（Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, OIRA）在完成審查時，認定這項規則[不具重大經濟影響](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eoDetails?rrid=1292261)。

支持者不但人數較少，立場也較狹窄：在約 2,900 則支持意見中，幾乎全都只提到防止浪費、詐欺與濫用（WFA），除此之外幾乎沒有其他理由；例如，[Immigration Accountability Project](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-12742) 讚揚這項規則新增要求聯邦補助受款人使用 E-Verify 系統。少數自行撰寫意見的支持者則提出較細緻的觀點，既支持降低 WFA，也建議修正；例如 [德州拉戈維斯塔市](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-36630) 提交的意見寫道：「本市支持改善聯邦支出監督的努力。然而，報銷程序的執行方式不應造成付款不必要的延遲……」

這些意見集中在少數幾項條文。第 [200.205](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.205) 條，也就是由政治任命官員在核發前審查裁量性補助案，受到最多關注，約有 6,900 則意見提及。第 [200.340](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.340) 條則位居第二，約有 5,900 則意見提及；該條擴大了終止執行中補助案的權限。其他經常被提及的條文則對可列支成本設下新限制，包括第 [200.461](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.461) 條與第 [200.432](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/read-the-rule#sec-200.432) 條（各自都有超過 3,000 則意見提及）。

## 公眾響亮的回應是斬釘截鐵的「不」，那接下來呢？

整體來看，這份紀錄相當驚人。數以萬計的科學家、臨床醫師與一般公民，用自己的話向美國管理及預算局（OMB）示警：若讓政治任命官員負責決定哪些研究能取得資助，將侵蝕聯邦資助科學的品質與獨立性。支持意見則少得多，也狹隘得多。依照通知與意見徵詢程序，OMB 現在必須審閱這些意見，並回應其中提出的每一項實質論點，才能發布最終規則。時程非常緊迫，從 7 月 13 日意見徵詢截止，到提議的 10 月生效日之間只有短短幾週，OMB 必須在這段時間內分析並回應意見。我們鼓勵審閱者[使用我們的工具來簡化分析。](https://omb-financial-assistance-comments.netlify.app/)

最後，當資訊與法規事務辦公室（OIRA）開始最終審查時，公眾應有機會依據第 12866 號行政命令，要求與 OMB 會面討論這項規則。有興趣的各方可留意 [reginfo.gov](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/eoPackageMain)，看看該選項是否會向公眾開放。

# 公眾反對 OMB 的聯邦財務援助規則

OMB 主任 Russell Vought 於 2026 年 6 月 30 日星期二，在雷本大樓出席眾議院撥款委員會金融服務暨一般政府小組委員會、就管理與預算局監督議題作證後現身。（Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images）

5 月 29 日，白宮管理與預算局（Office of Management and Budget, OMB）[提議全面修訂《聯邦法規彙編》第 2 篇第 200 部分](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/29/2026-10817/regulation-for-federal-financial-assistance)，這套規範通常稱為《聯邦財務援助統一指南》。自 2013 年以來，這套架構一直規範美國各聯邦機關如何在全國管理聯邦補助、合作協議與財務援助。受 2 CFR 200 規範的這類聯邦援助超過 1 兆美元，其中很大一部分流向支持州與地方政府、原住民族部落、大學、非營利組織、公共機構、學區、醫療組織、小型企業與研究機構的計畫，因此這項擬議規則的結果將影響美國經濟的一大部門。其中約 1,500 億美元援助是以研發補助形式提供，支撐美國對科學與科技的投資。

這項擬議規則試圖將原本屬於行政指引的文字，提升為具有拘束力、適用於整個政府的法規，並把規則制定權集中到 OMB 本身。關鍵條文包括：要求所有裁量性補助案在核發前，都必須由政治任命人員審查，以確保符合現任政府的政策優先事項。此外，這項提案也擴大各機關終止既有補助案的裁量權，並限制與特定外國實體合作時可取得的資金。

科學與學術社群對此表達廣泛憂慮，並組織倡議行動，凸顯這些變更對研究獨立性與行政穩定性造成的風險。[美國物理學會](https://www.aps.org/initiatives/advocate-amplify/policy/federal-grants-rule-change)與[美國地球物理聯盟](https://agu.quorum.us/campaign/163877/)等組織動員會員提交公開意見，並透過客製化平台協助公眾撰寫回應。

5 月 29 日至 7 月 9 日之間，約有 51,000 則意見被張貼到 [regulations.gov](https://www.regulations.gov/document/OMB-2026-0034-0001)（另有超過 200,000 則已收到、但尚未公開）。公眾情緒的結論很清楚，而且一面倒：約 94% 反對這項擬議規則，只有 6% 支持，標示為不明確的不到 1%。反對意見壓倒性地是草根自發，而不是組織動員。制式信只占所有意見約 16%（約 8,400 則意見，來自 210 個不同的行動），而反對意見中只有約八分之一來自制式信行動。相較之下，對這項規則的支持幾乎全是有組織的：近九成支持意見（約 2,500 則）來自單一制式信行動。反對者多半自己撰寫意見；支持者多半簽署同一份制式信。

留言者橫跨許多領域，但以個人為主：約 39,000 則意見（77%）來自無隸屬單位的個人，另有 7,900 則來自個別研究者與學者。約 3,300 則來自病患、家屬與健康倡議者。以數量來看，組織機構所占比例不高，但其聲量值得注意，包括科學與專業學會（約 70 個）、大學與研究機構（約 30 個），以及倡議型非營利組織（近 280 個）。至少 14 位民選官員的辦公室送出反對信，包括一封由 [Jamie Raskin 眾議員（民主黨，馬里蘭州）與 125 位共同連署人](https://www.regulations.gov/comment/OMB-2026-0034-38282)提出的信。Susan Collins 參議員（共和黨，緬因州）[直接寄給 OMB 主任 Russell Vought](https://www.appropriations.senate.gov/news/majority/sen-collins-asks-omb-to-withdraw-parts-of-grant-rule-extend-comment-period) 的信，並未納入這份彙整。
